assays.assay_name: Novelty-induced grooming in the open field (with locomotor tracking)
assays.assay_description: Rats placed immediately after i.p. injection into an unfamiliar 45 × 45 × 45 cm open-field arena and video-recorded for 30 min. Grooming was manually scored offline: traditional measures (total grooming time, bouts, latency) in Exp 1 (psilocybin 0.1–3.2 mg/kg) and Exp 2 (RS-127445 ± psilocybin 0.32 mg/kg), plus Grooming Analysis Algorithm microstructure (bout categories, stage transitions, head/body elements) in Exp 2. Locomotion (immobility, distance, moving time) tracked with EthoVision XT 15 and rearing scored manually as motor-confound controls in the same sessions.

application_type.evidence: intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of either saline or a single dose of psilocybin

setup_habituation.evidence: Immediately after the acute injection of psilocybin or saline, rats were placed in an unfamiliar open-field arena

setup_restrain.evidence: rats were placed in an unfamiliar open-field arena (45 × 45 × 45 cm), and their behavior was recorded with a camera for 30 min

Table 1: 'Three rats in this group [VEH-PSI] did not perform any Multiple-Area Bouts (MABs)... were excluded from the Grooming Analysis Algorithm (GAA)' (n=5 for GAA microstructure; min n=7 for traditional measures).

outcomes.summary: Psilocybin dose-dependently decreased total grooming time and number of grooming bouts (significant from 0.32 mg/kg) without affecting latency; at 1.0 and 3.2 mg/kg this was confounded by increased immobility, but not at 0.32 mg/kg. GAA microstructure showed 0.32 mg/kg psilocybin selectively reduced incorrectly initiated, interrupted and reversed-transition bouts and incorrect transitions (correct transitions rose from 18% to 61%), and RS-127445 reversed many of these effects while having no effect alone.
outcomes.statistics: Exp 1: grooming time H = 31.02, p < 0.0001; bouts F4,34 = 36.51, p < 0.0001; latency H = 1.53, p = 0.82; immobility H = 27.04, p < 0.0001. Exp 2: grooming duration H = 19.47, p < 0.001; bouts Antagonist F1,28 = 11.61, p < 0.01, Agonist F1,28 = 7.02, p < 0.05, interaction F1,28 = 1.66, p = 0.21; latency H = 2.94, p = 0.40; immobility Antagonist F1,28 = 0.64, p = 0.43, Agonist F1,28 = 1.07, p = 0.31. Microstructure (Table 1): incorrectly initiated bouts Agonist F1,25 = 34.06, p < 0.0001; total transitions H = 13.14, p < 0.01; percent correct transitions H = 12.17, p < 0.01.
outcomes.evidence: psilocybin dose-dependently decreased the total time spent grooming (H =31.02, p <0.0001; Fig. 2A) and the number of grooming bouts (F4,34 = 36.51, p < 0.0001; Fig. 2B) without affecting the latency to start grooming (H = 1.53, p = 0.82; Fig. 2C).

B1_num_measures.evidence: total grooming time, number of grooming bouts, latency to start grooming, immobility, distance, moving time, rearing, plus GAA bout categories, transition counts/percentages, and head/body elements (Table 1)

B2_temporal_dynamics.evidence: Crucially, both behavioral effects were reversed by pretreatment with RS-127445 (p < 0.05 for both measures; see Supplementary Fig. S3 for the timecourse).

B3_sequential_structure.evidence: grooming behavior was evaluated across three hierarchical dimensions: macro-level bout architecture, sequential transitional dynamics, and regional elements... Transitions between consecutive grooming stages were quantified
